title: A US order pushes DeepSeek out of civilian agencies, one hacker’s AI agents broke into more than 100 company websites, and GitHub retired six Copilot models. Anthropic says it will rewrite parts of its own AI safety bill, OpenAI’s newest models now migrate COBOL far more reliably, and Accenture caps staff Claude funding at $29 a month.
summary: Between 15 and 20 October 2026: the US Department of Homeland Security made public an order removing DeepSeek, and third-party products built on it, from federal civilian agency systems and purchasing. Security firm NorForge reported that a hacker’s AI agents, run on the open-source Cairn platform, broke into more than 100 websites for about $50 each. GitHub retired six models from Copilot, including GPT-5.5 and Grok 4.5. Anthropic confirmed it had shown Congress a draft frontier AI safety bill and said it would narrow the state-preemption language and revisit its thresholds. OpenAI reported that GPT-6.1 Sol passes 86.6% of its COBOL migration tests at low effort, up from 5.4%. Meta said a Claude tool’s rapid browsing triggered the suspension of the No Kings Coalition’s Instagram account, and WIRED found hidden WhatsApp chatbot instructions telling it not to recommend regulators. Disney is hiring most of bankrupt Character.AI’s staff and bidding $20 million for a licence to its technology. Schwab is blocking outside AI agents from moving client money, and Accenture now funds only $29 a month of Claude use per employee.
uncertainty: The DeepSeek order’s filed copy gives an original release date of 24 July 2026, while CyberScoop describes a letter dated 26 June; which products count as “developed using DeepSeek implementations” has not been spelled out. The Cairn campaign rests on NorForge’s report: The Next Web says it has not independently verified the intrusions, the token-cost figures are rough estimates, and Reuters could not establish how much data, if any, was taken. Anthropic’s bill text has not been published by the company and is still a draft with no sponsor. OpenAI’s COBOL and MultiLangBench results are its own evaluations. Meta has not named the Claude tool involved in the No Kings suspension or who ran it. WhatsApp says the exposed chatbot text was displayed because of a bug; how long it was visible is unclear. Disney’s bid can still be topped. Accenture’s $29 figure comes from an internal announcement seen by 404 Media, not a public policy.

stories.theme: US civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek, including tools built on it
stories.changed: On Monday 19 October 2026 the US Department of Homeland Security filed a notice, published in the Federal Register on Tuesday 20 October, of an order that bars federal civilian agencies from buying products and services from DeepSeek and its affiliates and requires them to remove DeepSeek products already in use. The order, signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, also covers third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations. The filed copy gives an original release date of 24 July 2026, so it has applied for months without being public. It cites data stored on servers in China, collection of personal information by DeepSeek-hosted apps, and the risk of sensitive data passing to China through prompts. Agencies could request an exception within 60 days of the order, with a compelling justification. It covers civilian agencies only; defence and intelligence systems fall under separate authorities.
stories.matters: Until now, US agencies blocked DeepSeek one by one at their own discretion. A single government-wide order that also reaches products built on DeepSeek turns model choice into a procurement question for every vendor selling software to US civilian agencies.
stories.imply: Which model sits inside a product is becoming a compliance question, not only a cost and quality one. If you sell to governments or regulated buyers, expect to be asked which models your product uses.
uses: List every model your product and internal tools call, including open-weight models you host yourself.
If you sell to US federal civilian agencies, ask counsel whether any DeepSeek-based feature needs to be removed or swapped.
Keep a tested fallback model for any feature built on DeepSeek, so a customer or government ban does not break it.
stories.example: A software firm with a US agency customer finds that its document-search feature calls DeepSeek through a third-party API. It moves that feature to another model for government accounts and records the change in its compliance file.
stories.audience: Government contractors, procurement and compliance teams, CTOs, and anyone whose product uses DeepSeek models.
stories.watch: How agencies read “third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations”, especially for self-hosted open weights. Whether other Chinese models are added. Whether US states or allied governments follow.

source.title: CyberScoop: DHS to ban DeepSeek from federal civilian agencies, 19 October 2026
source.quote: The order requires civilian agencies to exclude DeepSeek products from future procurements while removing any versions that might have been put in place prior to the ban.

stories.theme: Anthropic wrote its own AI safety bill, and now says parts need rewriting
stories.changed: On Friday 16 October 2026 Politico reported that Anthropic had been privately showing members of Congress the text of a federal frontier AI safety bill, and Anthropic confirmed it reflects its Advanced AI Framework. Under the draft, the government could block a model’s release or use only if it posed a risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damage, from a bioweapon, a cyberattack or a lab losing control of a model, and only through a federal judge in Washington DC acting on a request from the Commerce Department. Registered independent evaluators, who may be paid by the labs, would assess them and report imminent risks within 72 hours. The draft would also override some state laws, such as California’s. On Sunday 18 October Anthony Cimino, who leads Anthropic’s federal affairs team, said the company plans to update the preemption language so states keep a role, and that it is “probably time to re-evaluate thresholds”. No member of Congress has introduced the bill, and Congress is out of session until after the November midterms.
stories.matters: It is one of the most detailed AI law texts a frontier lab has put in front of Congress, and it shows what a federal regime could demand of the companies whose tools you use: published risk reports, outside evaluators and incident reporting. The preemption fight decides whether state laws such as California’s keep applying.
stories.imply: Federal AI safety rules in the US are still a draft-stage argument. For now, state laws and your vendors’ own published safety reports are the rules that actually apply.
uses: Ask your main AI vendors for their latest published safety or risk reports and keep them with your vendor assessment.
If you operate in California or New York, keep tracking state AI safety duties rather than waiting for a federal law.
Add questions on independent evaluation and incident reporting to your AI procurement checklist now.
stories.example: A bank’s AI governance team adds two questions to its vendor review: who independently evaluates the model, and how quickly the vendor tells customers about a safety incident.
stories.audience: Policy, legal and compliance teams, AI governance leads, and anyone buying frontier AI services.
stories.watch: A revised draft with narrower preemption and new thresholds. Whether any member of Congress sponsors it after the midterms. Responses from other labs and state lawmakers.

source.title: Tom’s Hardware: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line, 18 October 2026
source.quote: This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June

stories.theme: Six models disappeared from GitHub Copilot on Monday
stories.changed: On Monday 19 October 2026 GitHub removed six models from most Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions: Gemini 3.7 Flash, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 mini, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4.5. The retirements were announced on 18 September. GitHub’s suggested replacements are Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6.1 Sol (for GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.4), GPT-6 Luna (for the two mini models) and Grok 4.7. GitHub asks users to update workflows and integrations, and says Copilot Enterprise administrators may need to enable the replacement models in their model policies before staff can choose them.
stories.matters: Model lifetimes are now measured in months. Any script, automation or team guide that names a specific model can stop working, and in a company the replacement may sit switched off until an admin acts.
stories.imply: Treat model names like software versions with an end-of-life date. Someone on the team should own the list of models you depend on.
uses: Search your repositories, CI configs and automations for the six retired model names and switch to the suggested replacements.
If you administer Copilot Enterprise, check that GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.7 are enabled in model policies.
Re-run a few standard tasks on the replacement model to catch changes in output quality or cost.
stories.example: A platform team finds “gpt-5.5” hard-coded in its code-review bot. It moves the bot to GPT-6.1 Sol, enables the model in Copilot policy and compares a week of reviews with the old ones.
stories.audience: Developers, engineering managers and Copilot administrators.
stories.watch: The next deprecation notice on GitHub’s changelog. Whether the replacements cost more per request. Similar retirements in other coding tools.

stories.theme: OpenAI says its newest models can now migrate COBOL far more reliably
stories.changed: On Monday 19 October 2026 OpenAI published results showing large gains for its latest models in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran and Visual Basic. On its COBOL migration test, which converts programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python or Rust and requires byte-for-byte matching outputs, GPT-6.1 Sol scored 86.6% at low reasoning effort, against 5.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol, at 61% of the API cost; at higher effort it reached 97.9%. On MultiLangBench, where a model builds a SQLite-compatible database engine in 20 languages, GPT-6 Astra averaged 87.4%, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with COBOL still the hardest at 72%. OpenAI is releasing the MultiLangBench test suite on GitHub and asking enterprise customers which languages and workflows to tackle next.
stories.matters: Banks, insurers and governments still run core systems on COBOL, and modernisation is slow mainly because the business rules live only in old code. A model that preserves behaviour during migration could cut the cost and risk of those projects.
stories.imply: These are OpenAI’s own tests, and OpenAI says production use still needs expert review and testing against the system’s business rules. Treat it as a faster migration assistant, not an autopilot.
uses: Pick one small, well-tested COBOL or Visual Basic program and run a pilot migration, checking outputs against the original.
Ask the model to write plain-English documentation of business rules buried in old code before anyone migrates it.
Look up the published MultiLangBench results for the languages you use to see where the models still fall short.
stories.example: An insurer’s IT team asks GPT-6.1 Sol to document and migrate a premium-calculation module to Java, then compares the new code’s outputs against a year of real transactions before it goes near production.
stories.audience: CIOs, mainframe and legacy-system teams, and IT leaders in banking, insurance and government.
stories.watch: Independent results on real legacy codebases. What long migration jobs cost in practice. Whether other labs publish comparable numbers.

source.title: OpenAI: Advancing coding in low-resource programming languages, 19 October 2026
source.quote: On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less.

stories.theme: One hacker let AI agents break into more than 100 company websites
stories.changed: On Monday 19 October 2026 security firm NorForge published findings, reported by Reuters and The Verge, that a Chinese-speaking hacker used Cairn, an open-source AI agent platform, to break into more than 100 websites with little human involvement. Reuters identified victims including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. Since 25 September the attacker’s agents had tried more than 1,200 sites, mostly online shops in the US, Canada, Japan and Australia, working from instructions of fewer than 100 Chinese characters; successful break-ins took a little under 23 hours on average. NorForge’s researcher estimated about $5,000 in AI tokens for the campaign, roughly $50 per successful hack. The activity came to light because more than 20 Cairn control panels judged likely malicious were left open on the internet. Deere said it saw no sign that sensitive data was accessed, SharkNinja said a standalone product-support site was hit, and Cummins said it was investigating a possible attack on a vendor’s website.
stories.matters: By one researcher’s estimate, a patient, persistent break-in now costs about $50 in AI tokens. Small, forgotten company sites, vendor-run pages and support portals are exactly what these agents probe, around the clock.
stories.imply: Your attack surface includes every site with your name on it, including those run by agencies and vendors. Patching speed and visibility matter more when one attacker can try a thousand targets at once.
uses: List every public website and subdomain tied to your brand, including those run by vendors, and retire the ones nobody owns.
Ask web vendors when they last patched their platforms and whether they watch for web shells and unexpected file uploads.
If your team runs AI agent tools, make sure their control panels are never exposed to the open internet.
stories.example: An appliance brand finds an old product-support microsite still running on a vendor’s unpatched server. It takes the site down, moves the support pages to its main domain and adds the vendor to quarterly security reviews.
stories.audience: Security and IT teams, e-commerce managers, marketing teams that run microsites, and vendor managers.
stories.watch: Whether hosting firms take the exposed panels down. Data-loss disclosures from victims. Whether agent platforms add abuse controls.

source.title: The Verge: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents, 19 October 2026
source.quote: A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge.

stories.theme: A Claude tool’s browsing got a protest group’s Instagram suspended, Meta says
stories.changed: On Sunday 18 October 2026 Andy Stone, Meta’s vice-president of communications, said the No Kings Coalition’s Instagram account was taken offline on Saturday 17 October, the day of nearly 3,000 pre-midterm events across the US, because Meta’s security systems detected “a Claude tool” reading profiles, posts and hashtags at about four times the usual volume in intense bursts. The pattern looked like bot traffic rather than a person browsing. This replaced Meta’s first explanation, which blamed very frequent posting and commenting. An automated re-review restored the account about an hour later, but its admins were locked out for longer; the coalition says it was down for about 90 minutes. Meta apologised, but did not say which Claude tool was involved, who ran it or what it was doing.
stories.matters: Agents that browse on your behalf with your logged-in accounts look like bots to platforms’ anti-abuse systems. For a business, that can mean losing a social, ad or marketplace account at the worst possible moment.
stories.imply: Before an agent uses a company account, assume the platform may treat it as automation and penalise the account, not the agent.
uses: Keep agents off your main brand social accounts; use official APIs or a separate research account instead.
Limit how fast and how often any agent or automation reads from a platform, and avoid running several at once on one login.
Make sure at least two people have admin and recovery access to every important social and ad account.
stories.example: A marketing team that uses an AI agent to monitor competitors’ posts moves it to a separate account, slows its request rate and keeps the brand account for people only.
stories.audience: Social media, marketing and community managers, and anyone running AI agents on logged-in accounts.
stories.watch: Whether Meta or Anthropic identify the tool. Whether platforms publish rules for agent access to logged-in accounts. More suspensions as personal agents spread.

source.title: The Next Web: Meta says a Claude AI tool triggered the No Kings Instagram suspension, 19 October 2026
source.quote: The engineers at Meta stated that the Claude tool read profiles, posts, and hashtags at about four times the speed of a normal person, in brief, intense bursts.

stories.theme: WhatsApp’s hidden chatbot rules told it not to point users to regulators
stories.changed: On Monday 19 October 2026 WIRED reported that around 80 WhatsApp help and FAQ pages had exposed about 100 blocks of hidden instructions meant for Meta’s support chatbot, found by privacy company Redact. On the page about deleting an account, the instructions said: “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority.” Others told the bot not to cite WhatsApp’s terms of service or privacy policy, or data protection laws such as GDPR, LGPD or CCPA, “including when a user raises them directly”, and set rules for when a user mentions lawyers or lawsuits. After WIRED contacted Meta the text was removed; a WhatsApp spokesperson said a bug caused it to be displayed and that the chatbot is meant to help users with WhatsApp, not give legal advice.
stories.matters: Customer-service chatbots follow instructions customers never see. This is a rare look at how those instructions can steer people away from their rights, and a reminder that users, journalists and regulators may one day read yours.
stories.imply: Write chatbot instructions as if they will be published. If a rule would embarrass you in a news story, or clash with consumer or data protection law, change it.
uses: Review your support bot’s instructions with legal and compliance, especially anything about complaints, refunds, regulators or legal threats.
Make sure the bot hands people to a human or an official channel when they raise legal or data-rights questions, rather than stonewalling.
Check that internal prompt text is not leaking into public page code, help-centre exports or search indexes.
stories.example: A telecom’s compliance team audits its support bot and rewrites a rule that blocked any mention of the ombudsman. The bot now gives the official complaints route when a customer asks.
stories.audience: Customer-service leaders, compliance and legal teams, privacy officers and product managers who own chatbots.
stories.watch: Whether EU data protection authorities respond. Whether Meta explains how long the text was visible. Similar leaks from other companies’ help centres.

source.title: WIRED: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot, 19 October 2026
source.quote: Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority

stories.theme: Disney takes Character.AI’s people and tech, but not its users or lawsuits
stories.changed: Bankruptcy court filings reported on 18 and 19 October 2026 set out Disney’s deal with Character.AI, which filed for Chapter 11 on 12 October. Disney agreed to offer jobs to up to six key employees, including the chief executive, and at least 60 more. It estimates their yearly pay at about $60 million and will fund a $30 million retention pool, about $180 million over three years in total. Separately, Disney is the opening bidder, at $20 million, for a permanent, non-exclusive licence to Character.AI’s training systems and safety tools, including its age-prediction model; the licence excludes finished models, user data, training data and the brand. Disney required the deal to go through a Chapter 11 sale and takes on none of the company’s liabilities, which include lawsuits and child-safety investigations. Rival bids are due by 20 November. If no buyer emerges or the court rejects the deal, Character.AI will wind down the platform.
stories.matters: When an AI start-up fails, its people and code can be sold separately from its product and its users’ data. If your company relies on a small AI vendor, the tool could close while the team moves on.
stories.imply: Vendor risk for AI tools now includes legal risk, not just funding risk. Know what happens to your data and service if a supplier is sold or shut down.
uses: For each smaller AI vendor you rely on, check the contract for data return, deletion and continuity terms if the company is sold or closes.
Export and keep copies of the prompts, conversations and configurations that matter to your business.
Ask key AI suppliers about pending lawsuits and regulatory investigations as part of due diligence.
stories.example: A customer-experience team piloting a chatbot from a small start-up adds a clause requiring 30 days’ notice and a full data export if the vendor is acquired or winds down.
stories.audience: Procurement, vendor-risk and legal teams, and anyone building on AI start-ups.
stories.watch: Whether a rival bidder appears by 20 November. What happens to Character.AI users’ chats if the platform closes. More acqui-hires through bankruptcy courts.

source.title: The Next Web: Disney to spend $180M on Character.AI staff over three years, filing shows, 19 October 2026
source.quote: Disney required that the transaction be fully consummated in a chapter 11 sale process.

stories.theme: Schwab blocks outside AI agents from moving client money
stories.changed: On Friday 16 October 2026 Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster told Bloomberg Television that Schwab is blocking unauthorised outside AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, that try to move clients’ money. He gets a weekly report on the blocks, and said the big agents are stopped in the tens and twenties each week. The problem, he said, is clients handing their passwords to an agent that then acts for them. Instead, Schwab will set up MCP servers, controlled connections that let a client’s chosen AI tool check balances and do research but not move money, and wants clients to use its own assistant, Charley. Earlier that week JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon said the bank would not let outside AI agents act inside its systems.
stories.matters: Personal agents that book, buy and pay are arriving faster than the rules on who is liable when they get it wrong. Large banks are answering with read-only access, which limits what agents can do with financial accounts for now.
stories.imply: Expect a split between “look” and “act” permissions for agents in finance. Agents that need to move money will have to go through official, bank-controlled channels.
uses: Never give an AI agent the password to a company bank or brokerage account; use official read-only connections where they exist.
If you build finance features with agents, design for read-only data access and a human approval step for every payment.
Check your bank’s terms on third-party access before connecting any AI tool to company accounts.
stories.example: A small firm’s finance lead wants an agent to reconcile spending. She connects it through the bank’s read-only feed and keeps all payments in the bank’s own app with two-person approval.
stories.audience: Finance and treasury teams, fintech product managers, and anyone experimenting with personal AI agents.
stories.watch: When Schwab’s MCP servers launch and what they allow. How regulators settle the liability question. Whether other banks publish agent-access rules.

source.title: The Next Web: Schwab and JPMorgan are blocking AI agents from moving customer money, 16 October 2026
source.quote: We can’t control it, the client can’t control it, something could go wrong and who’s liable?

stories.theme: Accenture now funds only $29 a month of Claude use per employee
stories.changed: From 1 October 2026 Accenture centrally funds only $29 a month per employee for Claude use, according to an internal announcement reported by 404 Media on Thursday 15 October. All costs are consumption-based: anything above $29 must be charged to a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), Accenture’s budget code for a specific project or team, and staff were warned that a WBS and a licence do not guarantee ongoing access. Licences are reviewed periodically and may be moved to where they bring the most value. Some employees had been spending up to $1,000 a month, and one said their Claude access had been revoked. Premium plans include $250 of token usage a week, but many staff are on the General plan. An Accenture spokesperson said the company makes AI available to all its people and aims to provide “the right tool for the right work”.
stories.matters: The AI spending crackdown has reached one of the world’s largest AI consultancies. When token costs land on project budgets, every heavy AI user needs a business case, and AI use becomes a cost clients may see.
stories.imply: Unlimited AI seats are ending at big employers. Teams that can show what their AI spending produces will keep access; others may lose it.
uses: Track your own or your team’s monthly AI usage and cost so you can justify it before anyone asks.
Agree with finance which project or cost centre pays for heavy AI use, and set alerts before limits are reached.
Match the tool to the task: use cheaper models or plans for routine work and keep premium seats for the work that needs them.
stories.example: A delivery lead at a consultancy shows that Claude Code cut a client project’s testing time by a third, and the client agrees to fund a premium seat from the project budget.
stories.audience: Managers, finance and procurement teams, consultants, and heavy AI users at large companies.
stories.watch: Whether other consultancies and large employers set similar caps. Whether AI vendors respond with cheaper enterprise plans. How caps change client project pricing.
